newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra's budget boost seen as pre-election gift.
newsitem.headline: Canberra's budget boost seen as pre-election gift.

text.p: The Australian government said on Wednesday its budget was in better shape than it had thought, creating speculation that it might be planning a pre-election spending spree.
The finance ministry announced that the government's accounts were A$4.934 billion in underlying deficit at June 30, almost A$2 billion better than estimated only two months ago.
The preliminary figures also showed the 1996/97 budget delivered a headline surplus of A$2.514 billion, over three times the A$764 million surplus estimate released in May.
The headline surplus includes one-off windfalls like the proceeds of asset sales and early repayment of loans to states. Financial markets look more closely at the underlying position.

"We haven't had any detailed figures yet, but I suspect the answer is that, because most of the improvement has been in the underlying (deficit), it's providing a substantially better base in 1997/98," Macquarie Bank chief economist Bill Shields said.
Treasurer Peter Costello confirmed this could be the case, but said even the improvement in the underlying deficit could reflect one-off benefits which would be lost in 1997/98.
"It may not feed into the 1997/98 year but if it indicates the base has improved, the budget position could improve in 1997/98," Costello told a new conference in Melbourne.
The government will not update its budget forecasts for current and future fiscal years until the mid-year fiscal review, due later in calendar 1997 or early 1998.
But economists said that if the preliminary improvement in the 1996/97 budget held up, Canberra could find itself in a better position to fight the next election, due by May 1999.
The next budget is due to be announced in May 1998 and would be the last before the next election. Political commentators are tipping an election in late 1998.
"As sure as night follows day, there will be either some type of tax cut or some pork-barrel spending...that will be announced in the May budget," ANZ Bank chief economist Saul Eslake told Reuters.
Costello, who has led an austerity drive to put the underlying budget into black by 1998, could choose not to squander any windfall improvement to the budget position.
But Eslake was not counting on it.
"If Costello has a A$2 billion honey-pot in there, you can bet the government is not going to see any votes in whacking that in the surplus," Eslake said.
